analysis: The photographs confirm this is the real thing and it is the best Maine buy in the sale. It is a genuine Carroll Thayer Berry colour woodblock of Bass Harbor Light on the Maine coast, pencil-titled BASS HARBOR LIGHT - MAINE COAST along the lower margin, pencil-signed Carroll Thayer Berry at the right and annotated 'imp' -- meaning he pulled the impression himself rather than having it printed commercially. The cut CTB monogram is in the block at lower left. The green-and-black two-block scheme is his characteristic palette. This earns its place on regional desirability rather than age, exactly as the brief allows, and Bass Harbor Light is one of the most recognisable subjects on the coast.
problems: There is visible foxing -- scattered orange-brown spots through the sky and into the margins. That is the condition-discount opportunity in its purest form: the market marks foxed paper down hard, but at normal viewing distance on a wall it reads as age rather than damage. Do check whether the spots are surface foxing or have gone through the sheet, and be aware the mat is likely acidic and should be replaced. The frame is a plain mid-century gilt moulding, adequate but not adding value.
patience: Moderate. Berry woodblocks appear regularly at Maine sales, which is precisely why you should not overpay -- but signed, artist-printed impressions of named lighthouse subjects are the desirable end of his output.
sources: Signature, title and 'imp' annotation read directly off the lot photographs.

analysis: The second of four Carroll Thayer Berry woodblocks running consecutively at $300-500 estimates. Four at once from one consignor is the classic exhaustion setup -- the two or three people in the room who want a Berry will have bought by the third lot, and the fourth is where the value sits. Bid all four in sequence and let the room tell you which one comes cheap.
problems: Apply the same checks as 3347: pencil signature and title in the margin, the block-cut monogram, and 'imp' if he printed it. An unsigned impression, or one signed only in the block, is worth substantially less. Foxing is endemic across this group.
patience: Moderate, and improved by having four chances in a row.

analysis: Third of the four Berry woodblocks, estimated $300-500. Same case as 3348 -- the value is in the sequence position rather than in any difference between the images.
problems: Same signature, condition and foxing checks. Compare the four subjects at preview and rank them before the sale starts, so that when the room thins out you already know which one you are prepared to take.

analysis: The last of the four consecutive Berry woodblocks, at a slightly higher $400-500 estimate. Being last is an advantage for you: by this point the Berry buyers have committed elsewhere. If any of the four is going to fall through the estimate, statistically it is this one.
problems: The higher estimate suggests a better subject or better condition -- establish which. Same checks throughout: pencil signature, pencil title, 'imp', foxing.

analysis: A late 19th-century watercolour of Maine, unsigned, at $300-400. This is the quiet ideal of the brief: it genuinely satisfies the hundred-year criterion, it is Maine subject matter, and because it is anonymous there is no maker premium to pay. The brief specifically identifies unsigned period regional work as the place where the budget buys something real, and this is that lot.
problems: Unsigned means the attribution rests entirely on the paper, the pigments and the framing, so verify the age claim at preview rather than taking it. Watercolours of this period are usually light-faded -- compare the exposed image with the strip under the mat edge to see how much colour has been lost. Check for foxing and for an acidic backing board.
patience: Moderate. Anonymous period Maine views are not rare, but they are consistently undervalued and this one is catalogued to the century.

analysis: George M. Hathaway (1852-1903) was a Portland marine painter and one of the genuinely antique Maine artists in a section otherwise dominated by living and mid-century painters. His dates put the work comfortably before 1926 on any reading, so this satisfies the antique criterion and the Maine criterion simultaneously -- a combination that is rarer in this sale than it looks.
problems: The $700-900 estimate is near the top of the budget band, so the margin for error is thin. Hathaway's quality varies and the market for minor 19th-century Maine marine painters is regional and shallow. Check the canvas for relining and the surface for overpaint in the sky, which is where marine paintings are most often restored.
patience: Low to moderate. Period Maine marine painters with dates this early are the scarce end of the regional market.

analysis: Charles E. Duncan Rodrick (1874 to about 1940) is an early Maine painter whose working life straddles the antique line, at a $300-400 estimate. Cheap, local, and old enough that some of his output genuinely clears a hundred years -- which makes the date of the individual picture worth establishing rather than assuming.
problems: The dating is inferred from the artist's active period, not from the picture, so it is an argument rather than a fact. Look for a date on the work itself. Rodrick is a minor name with a thin comparable record, so the estimate is the house's guess as much as anything.

analysis: William Sterna Barrett (1854-1927) worked in New York and Maine and died just after the antique line, so a mature work has a genuine chance of predating 1926. At $300-500 with five photographs this is worth examining as a possible antique-plus-Maine double hit.
problems: Straddles the line, so the status is honestly border rather than antique. As with Rodrick, look for a date on the canvas. Minor artists with dual-state associations are often catalogued to whichever state sells better, so confirm the Maine connection is actually reflected in the subject.

analysis: Alan Magee at a $200-300 estimate is the cheapest entry to a genuinely collected contemporary Maine name. Magee is a serious figure in the state's art world and his originals run into five figures, so anything of his at $200 is a print. That is fine -- the brief's whole point about Maine art is that works on paper by properly collected artists sit in band while the paintings do not.
problems: Establish the process and the edition. Magee has made lithographs, screenprints and reproductions, and the gap between a signed limited edition and an open-edition poster is the whole value. Check for a pencil signature and edition fraction below the image.
patience: Moderate. Magee prints appear regularly at Maine sales.

analysis: The companion Magee at $300-400, immediately after 3397 and immediately before four Magee originals estimated $10,000-12,000 each. Being the cheap lot standing in front of a wall of five-figure estimates is a good position: the room's attention is on what comes next.
problems: Same process and edition questions as 3397. The presence of the expensive originals in the same run may actually pull bidding up on the prints through association -- watch for that and stay disciplined.

analysis: Laurence Sisson is one of the names the brief specifically flags to watch, and this is the cheaper of the two Sissons in the sale at $500-700 against 3441's $1,000-1,500. Sisson's Maine coastal subjects have a steady regional following and his market is solid without being fashionable.
problems: The medium is not stated. Sisson worked in oil, casein and watercolour and the values differ substantially. Establish which before bidding, and check for the fading that affects his works on paper.
patience: Moderate to high. Sisson appears at most Maine sales, which argues against stretching.

analysis: Attributed to Charles Herbert Woodbury at $300-400. The Ogunquit colony founder at a tenth of his usual price, and the word doing all the work is 'attributed'. Per the standing principles this is a hopeful label rather than an attribution and should be priced as the anonymous work it currently is.
problems: If it were signed and certain, it would not be $300. Ask what the attribution rests on. Note this is the second Woodbury question in the sale alongside lot 1110 on Day 1 -- worth resolving both at the same preview visit. Priced as an anonymous period coastal work it is fine; priced as a Woodbury it is a mistake.
patience: High. Woodbury attributions of this kind are common and rarely firm up.

analysis: Juanita Stephens of Machias at $200-400 is hyper-local downeast material -- a named artist from a named small Maine town, which is exactly the kind of thing that sells to a committed regional audience and almost nowhere else. The cheaper of the two Stephens lots.
problems: Hyper-local also means thin resale: outside eastern Maine there is effectively no market. Buy it because you want it on the wall, not because it holds value. Check condition, since work by regional artists is often unframed or badly framed.

analysis: Harold Condon (1892-1934) at $250-350 is one of the cheapest early-dated Maine artists in the sale. His short working life means everything he made falls in the 1910s to early 1930s, so a portion of his output genuinely predates the antique line.
problems: Died young and left a small body of work with a correspondingly thin market record, so the estimate is guesswork. Straddles the antique line, so status is border. Look for a date on the picture.

analysis: Donald Sutherland of Eastport, Maine pottery at $600-800. Studio pottery from a named Maine maker with a specific town is local material with a genuine following among Maine craft collectors.
problems: The estimate is high for studio pottery generally -- the brief's caution about contemporary studio ceramics applies, and Day 1 carries a whole run of them that will help calibrate. Check for a maker's mark and for the firing and glaze faults that are common in reduction-fired work.
patience: High. Maine studio pottery is well supplied.

analysis: An Old Town canoe at $500-700. Old Town Canoe Company of Old Town, Maine is one of the state's great industrial names and a wood-and-canvas Old Town is a genuinely iconic Maine object. The catalogue says antique without committing to a date, but Old Town's serial numbers are documented and the company will date a hull from its number -- which makes this one of the few lots in the sale whose age can be established definitively rather than argued.
problems: Find the serial number on the inside stem at preview; the build records survive and that converts an unverified claim into a catalogued fact. Wood-and-canvas canoes need the canvas checked for rot, the ribs for cracks and the stems for softness. A canoe needing recanvassing costs more to restore than it is worth. Also be honest about storage -- this is sixteen feet of object.
patience: Moderate. Old Towns appear regularly in Maine but sound original ones at this money are the better end.

analysis: A large carved wooden trout trade sign stamped F&S at $300-500 is the only trade sign in Day 3 that sits inside the budget -- every other one runs $800 to $2,500. Trade signs are the strongest folk-art category in this part of the sale and a fish sign has natural coastal-Maine appeal. The F&S stamp is a lead worth chasing since a documented maker changes the picture entirely.
problems: The catalogue gives no date. Carved fish signs are reproduced in quantity for the decorating trade and the tells are a too-even carving, modern screws, and paint that sits on rather than in the surface. Period signs show weathering that follows the grain, old nail holes from repeated hanging, and paint layers that have checked. One photograph is thin disclosure for a $400 object.
patience: Low to moderate. Affordable trade signs are genuinely scarce -- the category has been strong for years and prices reflect it.

analysis: A White's Utica stoneware advertising canteen at $200-300. Advertising stoneware sits at the intersection of two collecting categories and White's of Utica is a documented pottery, so the maker is real even if the date is not stated.
problems: No date claim from the house. Check the cobalt decoration is period brushwork rather than a later transfer or a modern reproduction -- White's pieces have been copied. Hairlines and base chips are usual in stoneware and only matter if they go through.

analysis: Pierre-Jules Mene is the most commercially successful of the French animalier sculptors and this is the pick of the Day 3 bronze run on price -- $600-800 against Barye at $1,000-2,000. A genuine period Mene sand cast is a real named-maker antique and would be excellent value at this money.
problems: That is exactly why the category is a minefield. Mene's models were recast continuously after his death in 1879 and again through the 20th century, and later casts carry the same signature because it is cast into the model. The tells are in the chasing and the surface: period casts show crisp hand-finished detail in the fur and mane, a rich layered patina that varies with the form, and a smooth well-finished underside. Late casts are soft in the detail, uniformly dark, and often rough or unfinished underneath. Check for a foundry mark and weigh it in your hand -- period sand casts are heavier than they look.
patience: High for the recasts, which are everywhere. Low for genuine period casts -- but you must establish which you are looking at first.

analysis: Jules Moigniez at $500-700 is the cheapest of the French animalier bronzes and Moigniez is a properly documented name, particularly for birds. Note the catalogue has his dates backwards -- printed as 1935-1894, which should read 1835-1894. A small error, but it tells you the cataloguing on this run is not specialist work.
problems: The same recasting problem as the Mene, and Moigniez is if anything more heavily reproduced because his bird models are decorative. Apply the identical test: chasing quality, patina depth, underside finish, foundry marks. Moigniez's originals were often gilt-bronze, so a plain brown patina on a Moigniez is itself worth questioning.

analysis: Rosa Bonheur at $600-800. Bonheur is the most famous name in the animalier group and the one with the widest general recognition, which in a saleroom is a liability rather than an asset -- the room will bid the name.
problems: Bonheur's sculptural output is small and much of what carries her signature is a later cast or an outright commercial reproduction. Given the standing principle about suspiciously cheap headline names, treat a $600 Rosa Bonheur bronze as a red flag first and an opportunity second. Same physical tests as the other bronzes in the run.

analysis: Four pieces of Tiffany sterling flatware, all carrying the 1907-1947 date mark: three in St. Dunstan with monograms -- dinner fork, serving spoon and a small round-bowl serving spoon -- plus a Palm pattern sauce ladle with an MGE monogram. The date mark straddles 1926, so border rather than modern. 10.12 ozt is 315 g, roughly $455 of sterling and $396 after a refiner, against a $400-600 estimate: metal covers the low estimate outright, and St. Dunstan is one of Tiffany's better patterns.
problems: Monogrammed, which the market discounts and this buyer should not. Mixed patterns, so it is four odd pieces rather than a set. The 1907-1947 window cannot be narrowed from the mark alone.
patience: Moderate. Tiffany flatware appears regularly but rarely this cheap.

analysis: The catalogued weight turns this into the clearest metal-floor buy in the sale. A pair of cufflinks and three matching shirt studs, each an oval cabochon amethyst in a 14K yellow gold mount, all stamped, 7.2 dwt tw -- that is 11.2 g gross. Deducting generously for five cabochon amethysts leaves roughly 7.6-9.2 g of 14K, which at the brief's deliberately conservative $75.23 a gram is $572-692 of gold, or $497-602 after a refiner takes its 87%. The estimate is $300-400. Metal alone is worth more than the top estimate, and it is comfortably inside the band. Dress sets are deeply unfashionable, which is the only reason this is priced where it is -- and unfashionable-but-real is exactly what this collection is built to find.
problems: Amethyst is quartz and worth almost nothing; do not let the stones do any work in the valuation. The deduction above is deliberately generous to the stones, so the real gold content is probably higher, not lower. Confirm all five pieces are stamped 14K rather than four gold and one replaced -- mismatched dress sets are common. Cufflink backs and stud posts are sometimes base metal even on a gold set; they are a small fraction of the weight but check. If it runs past $560 the metal argument is gone.
patience: Moderate. Gold dress sets appear periodically and are consistently underbid.

analysis: An early 10K gold mourning brooch at $400-600. This hits three things at once: it is genuinely antique, it is gold, and per the standing principle 10K points to American rather than British manufacture, which localises it. Victorian mourning jewellery is also a proper collecting category with its own literature.
problems: 10K is only 41.7% gold at $53.63 a gram, so a 6-gram brooch holds about $320 of metal -- the estimate is at or slightly above melt, which is a reasonable place to be for an antique. Mourning brooches often contain hair work under glass; check the glass is intact and the compartment sealed, because once moisture gets in the hair work is finished. Check the pin and catch, which are frequently replaced.
patience: Moderate. Victorian mourning jewellery is a steady category but 10K American examples are less common than British 9K and 15K.

analysis: An antique 10K gold Masonic Egyptian Revival brooch at $700-900. Masonic jewellery has a dedicated collecting base independent of the gold, and the Egyptian Revival taste dates it to roughly the 1870s-1920s, which straddles the antique line.
problems: At the top of the budget band and 10K is the least gold-dense of the karats -- a brooch of this type might hold $250-400 of metal against a $700-900 estimate, so you are paying a substantial premium for the Masonic interest. That premium is real but it is not liquid. Confirm the karat mark and check for enamel losses, which are expensive to restore properly.

analysis: An E. Howard gold-filled open-face pocket watch with chain and box at $500-700. E. Howard is a genuinely important American watchmaker and the box and chain are a real plus, so this is not a bad object -- but read the metal description carefully.
problems: Gold-filled has no melt floor at all. It is a thin gold layer bonded over base metal and the word gold in the title implies value that is not there. What you are buying is the movement, and E. Howard movements vary enormously in grade -- the value difference between a low-grade and a high-grade Howard is several hundred dollars. Ten photographs suggests the movement is being shown; identify the grade and serial before bidding. Priced as a watch this may be fair; priced as gold it is a mistake.
patience: High. Pocket watches are a deep market with continuous supply.

analysis: Now underpinned by a catalogued weight. An 18K open-face pendant watch with an unsigned manual movement, white enamel dial with Roman numerals, and a finely engraved guilloche case back with a monogram cartouche -- 13.7 dwt tw, which is 21.3 g gross. A pendant watch case is thin and the movement, dial and crystal are not gold, so deducting 45-65% for those leaves roughly 7.5-11.7 g of 18K: $719-1,129 of gold at the brief's working price, $626-982 after a refiner. Against a $600-800 estimate the metal is at or above the low end, and the watch runs. Inside the band with a real floor under it.
problems: The movement is unsigned, so there is no horological name to add value -- this is a gold case with a watch in it, and it should be bought that way. Weigh the case separately at preview if the house will allow it, because the 45-65% deduction is the whole argument and it is my estimate, not theirs. Enamel dials chip at the winding hole and the edges; check under the bezel. 'Running at time of cataloging' is not the same as keeping time.

analysis: A Victorian gold and mother-of-pearl lorgnette dated 1850 at $600-800. The house has committed to a specific year, which is unusually precise and suggests an inscription. Comfortably antique, and lorgnettes are charming objects with a small dedicated following.
problems: Gold content is unstated -- 'gold' without a karat mark on Victorian jewellery often means low-karat or gold-filled mounts, so establish the actual fineness before treating this as a metal lot. Check the folding mechanism works and the lenses are present and uncracked; mother-of-pearl chips at the edges.

analysis: A 14K gold opal and diamond ring at $500-700 sits inside the budget, which makes it worth a specific warning rather than a silent screen.
problems: The brief's standing point applies directly: composite and doublet opals are worth far less relative to their gold content than solid stones, and a ring at this price with a substantial opal is a strong candidate for a doublet. Under magnification a doublet shows a flat join line at the girdle. The gold in a ring of this size is perhaps 3 to 5 grams -- $225 to $375 -- so the estimate assumes the stone carries real value. Verify the opal is solid before treating any of that as real.

analysis: A William Spratling sterling and rosewood trinket box at $400-600. Spratling was the American who revived the Taxco silver industry and his work is genuinely collected with a documented literature and a reliable market -- a named maker in the true sense rather than a retailer's stamp. Mid-century rather than antique, but this is one of the few named-maker silver objects in the sale inside the budget.
problems: Spratling's marks changed over his career and are extensively faked; learn the correct mark for the period before bidding. The rosewood is not silver, so do not calculate melt on gross weight -- the sterling content of a small box with a wooden body is modest. Check the wood for cracks and the hinge for repair.
patience: Moderate. Spratling appears periodically and holds value well.

analysis: A 19th-century Waterbury calendar regulator clock at $300-400 is one of the better plain-value lots in Day 3: catalogued to the century, a documented American clockmaker, and a calendar movement, which is the complication that makes a Waterbury worth having rather than just old.
problems: Establish whether the calendar mechanism works -- that is the whole point of the clock and repair is specialist and expensive. Check the case for veneer losses, the dial for repainting, and whether the movement and case belong together. Marriage of movement to case is endemic in American clocks.
patience: Moderate. American shelf and wall clocks are common but calendar models less so.

analysis: A Victorian hollow lead garden sculpture of a satyr at $400-600. Period lead garden ornament is a proper category with a real following, and lead weathers to a soft grey that reproductions never quite achieve.
problems: Hollow lead is structurally fragile and splits along its seams -- check for cracking and for previous repairs, which are usually crude. Lead is also soft enough to have been damaged by frost if it has held water. One photograph for a garden sculpture is not enough; this needs to be seen from all sides.

analysis: A matched pair of circa-1870 Victorian cast iron garden benches, catalogued to the period. Genuinely antique and a handsome thing, but the $1,500-2,000 estimate with a $750 opening puts it well outside the budget band.
problems: Beyond the price, cast iron garden furniture is heavily reproduced from original patterns and the reproductions are hard to distinguish once weathered. Period castings show crisper detail, hand-filed seam lines and layered paint history.

analysis: A Tiffany Studios lamp at $25,000-35,000 with a $12,000 opening. Listed here only to make the point the brief already makes: real Tiffany Studios is comprehensively outside this budget, and the six Tiffany Studios lots in Day 3 confirm what the price of the genuine article looks like.
problems: Useful as a calibration exercise at preview -- seeing what $25,000 of genuine Tiffany looks like is the best inoculation against paying $800 for something claiming to be near it.

analysis: The fifth Carroll Thayer Berry lot, estimated $12,000-15,000 against the $300-500 of the four woodblocks immediately before it. This will be a major oil rather than a print, and it is thirty times the budget ceiling.
problems: Its real significance for you is positional: it sits at the end of the Berry run, and a five-figure Berry crossing the block right after four cheap ones tends to concentrate the room's attention and money there. That is good for your chances on 3347 to 3350.

analysis: A Gladenbeck bronze and ivory figure at $750-1,000. Gladenbeck was a substantial Berlin foundry and chryselephantine figures of this type are properly of the period, so the object is likely right.
problems: The ivory element makes this the most constrained lot in the sale. Elephant ivory in combination with bronze is subject to federal Endangered Species Act restrictions on interstate commerce, and a figure at this price will not come with the documentation that would ease that. Ivory-mounted Deco and Nouveau figures are also the single most faked category in the decorative arts, with resin and bone substitutes routine. High price, high complication, high fake rate -- pass.

analysis: Tom Paiement of Bath, Maine -- the buyer's own town. There are two Paiement lots and this is the larger at $2,000-2,500, which is out of band; the point of flagging it is 3305 immediately after at $800-1,000, which is not.
problems: Contemporary and local means the market is essentially the artist's gallery price, so there is no discount to find and no scarcity to exploit. Buy on whether you want it, not on value. Out of band at this estimate.

analysis: The smaller Tom Paiement at $800-1,000, from an artist working in the buyer's own town of Bath. Purely a personal-collection purchase -- no antique claim, no scarcity argument, and the brief's Maine allowance is doing all the work.
problems: At the top of the budget band for a living local artist whose work can be bought from the studio. There is no value case here, only a preference case, and it should be treated as such.
patience: Very high -- the artist is alive and working twenty minutes away.
